sectionDirections.title: Section 1. Analogies
sectionDirections.text: Each item in this section consists of a series of words. The first word is related to the second in the same way as the third word is related to a fourth one which is missing. Select this missing word from the given choices.

example.note: There are other relationships involved in the items aside from that illustrated above.

meta.notes: Editable — add your own items following docs/question-format.md

questions.explanation: The relationship is creator to creation. An architect designs a building; an author writes a book. Library (A) is a place where books are kept, not something the author produces. Reader (C) is the audience who receives the work. Publisher (D) is a business that prints and sells the work, a separate role rather than the product. All three wrong choices are associated with an author, but only Book is what the author actually makes. Exam tip: NMAT distractors are often related words; the correct answer must repeat the exact relationship of the first pair.
questions.hint: Make a sentence: 'An architect makes a building, so an author makes a ___.' Choose the product, not the place, the audience, or the business.

questions.explanation: The relationship is instrument to the quantity it measures. A thermometer measures temperature; a barometer measures atmospheric (air) pressure. Every wrong choice is weather-related but belongs to a different instrument: humidity is measured by a hygrometer (A), wind speed by an anemometer (C), and altitude by an altimeter (D). A barometer can be used to estimate altitude, but its primary job is measuring air pressure. Memorize common instruments: seismograph (earthquakes), odometer (distance), speedometer (speed), hygrometer (humidity).
questions.hint: Use the sentence 'A ___ measures ___.' Know your instrument names: baro- relates to pressure. Reject choices that are weather terms but belong to other instruments.

questions.explanation: The relationship is reference work to what it is made up of. A catalog is a collection of entries for items; an atlas is a collection of maps. Countries (A) and roads (B) are things that maps show, but they are not what the atlas is physically composed of. Globes (D) are round models of the Earth and are not bound into an atlas. The trap is confusing what the book depicts with what the book contains.
questions.hint: Ask what the book itself is made of. A catalog is made of entries for items; an atlas is made of ___. Choose the unit inside the book, not the subject matter it covers.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what is the author's primary concern about antibiotic use in agriculture?
questions.passage: Low doses of antibiotics have been routinely added to livestock feed to promote growth and prevent disease in crowded conditions. Public health researchers warn that this practice accelerates the development of drug-resistant bacteria, which can spread from farms to humans through food, water, and direct contact. Several countries have restricted non-therapeutic antibiotic use, citing the need to preserve medications for human medicine.

choices.text: The rise of bacteria resistant to antibiotics
Shortages of veterinary staff on farms

questions.explanation: The concern is signaled by the word 'warn' in the second sentence: routine antibiotic use accelerates drug-resistant bacteria that can spread to humans. The last sentence supports this, since countries restrict the practice to preserve medicines for humans. Choices A, B, and D are never mentioned in the passage. Choice B is also contradicted, because antibiotics are described as promoting growth. Exam tip: for 'concern' or 'problem' questions, look for signal words such as warn, worry, risk, threat, and danger, and answer only from the text.
questions.hint: Find the signal word 'warn' and see what comes right after it. Eliminate any choice whose topic never appears in the passage.

questions.prompt: Which statement best summarizes the passage?
questions.passage: Placebo effects demonstrate that a patient's expectations can influence perceived symptoms even when no active drug is given. Modern clinical trials therefore compare new treatments against placebos to separate true pharmacological effects from psychological ones. Critics argue that placebo-controlled designs can withhold effective therapy, raising ethical questions in serious illnesses.

choices.text: Placebos cure most diseases when patients believe in them.
Expectations can affect symptoms, which shapes how trials are designed and debated.
All clinical trials should eliminate placebo groups immediately.
Psychological effects are stronger than any medication.

questions.explanation: A good summary covers the whole passage: (1) expectations influence symptoms, (2) trials use placebos because of this, (3) critics raise ethical concerns. Choice B captures all three. A overstates the passage, since placebos influence perceived symptoms and are not said to cure most diseases. C turns the critics' concern into an extreme demand ('all', 'immediately') that the passage never makes. D makes an unsupported comparison ('stronger than any medication'). Exam tip: absolute or extreme words (all, most, any, only, never, immediately) are red flags in summary and main-idea choices.
questions.hint: A summary must cover every paragraph or sentence. Cross out choices with extreme wording or claims the passage never makes.

questions.explanation: The relationship is antonyms. Ephemeral means short-lived and is the opposite of permanent. The blank is in the third position, so you need the opposite of stable. Volatile means liable to change rapidly or unpredictably, which is the opposite of stable. Fixed (A), solid (C), and constant (D) are all synonyms or near-synonyms of stable, so they repeat the idea instead of reversing it. Vocabulary note: volatile is also used for substances that evaporate easily and for unstable markets or tempers.
questions.hint: Read it as 'ephemeral is to permanent as ___ is to stable.' Because the first pair is opposites, find the opposite of stable and cross out every synonym.

questions.prompt: Which choice best captures the main idea of the passage?
questions.passage: Many cities are redesigning parks to include native plants and less manicured lawns. Supporters argue that this approach reduces water use, lowers maintenance costs, and creates habitats for pollinators. Critics worry that the resulting landscapes may look less formal and less familiar to residents.

choices.text: Cities are removing parks entirely to save money
New park designs balance ecological benefits with aesthetic concerns
Pollinators are harmful to urban spaces

questions.explanation: The passage presents benefits (less water, lower costs, pollinator habitats) and a concern (a less formal, less familiar look). The main idea must include both sides, which is what B does. A contradicts the passage, because parks are being redesigned, not removed. C overgeneralizes the critics' worry into a claim about all residents. D contradicts the passage, which presents pollinator habitats as a benefit. Exam tip: when a passage gives supporters' and critics' views, the main idea is usually a balanced statement; a choice covering only one side is incomplete.
questions.hint: Count how many viewpoints appear. If both supporters and critics speak, the main idea must reflect both. Reject choices that contradict a stated detail.

questions.explanation: The relationship is animal to its home or dwelling. A bird lives and raises its young in a nest; a bee colony lives in a hive. Flower (A) is a food source the bee visits, honey (B) is a product the bee makes, and pollen (D) is material the bee collects. All three are associated with bees, but none is where a bee lives. Related animal-to-home pairs worth memorizing: bee : hive, ant : colony or anthill, fox : den, horse : stable, spider : web.
questions.hint: Ask 'Where does the animal live?' Reject food, products, and materials, which are related to bees but are not homes.

questions.explanation: The relationship is antonyms. To abridge is to shorten a text by cutting parts of it, and its opposite is to lengthen. To reduce is to make smaller, and its opposite is to enlarge. Shrink (A), compress (C), and condense (D) are all synonyms of reduce, so they repeat the idea instead of reversing it. Exam tip: when the first pair is opposites, eliminate every choice that means the same as the third word. Here three of the four choices are synonyms, so only one can be the antonym.
questions.hint: Confirm the first pair is opposites. Then find the opposite of REDUCE and cross out the synonyms (three of the choices).

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what is the main benefit of hybrid work models for employees?
questions.passage: Many companies are adopting hybrid work schedules that combine remote and office days. Employees report greater flexibility and improved work-life balance, while employers see higher productivity and reduced overhead costs. Critics note that hybrid setups can blur personal boundaries if expectations are not managed clearly.

choices.text: Lower real estate costs for employers.

questions.explanation: The second sentence gives two groups their own benefits: employees get flexibility and improved work-life balance, and employers get productivity and reduced overhead costs. The question asks about employees, so B is correct. A is a trap: reduced overhead is an employer benefit. C and D are not stated as benefits anywhere in the passage. Exam tip: when a passage mentions several groups, check who the question is asking about before choosing.
questions.hint: Ask 'for whom?' Underline the group named in the question and match it to the benefit stated for that same group.

questions.explanation: The relationship is antonyms. Penurious means extremely poor (or stingy) and wealthy is its opposite. Arid means very dry, so its opposite is humid, meaning containing a lot of moisture. Dry (B) is a synonym of arid. Barren (C) describes land that produces nothing, a typical result of aridity rather than its opposite. Fertile (D) is the opposite of barren and describes soil productivity, not moisture. Always compare on the same scale: arid and humid sit at opposite ends of the dryness-moisture scale.
questions.hint: First confirm the pair is antonyms. Then find the choice that is the opposite on the same scale as ARID (dry vs. moist). Cross out the synonym first.

questions.prompt: What does the author imply is the main benefit of reusable packaging?
questions.passage: Reusable packaging cuts waste by keeping containers in circulation instead of discarding them after a single use. Companies that invest in refillable systems report lower waste management costs and stronger customer loyalty. While critics note the initial expense, supporters say the long-term environmental and financial savings outweigh the upfront investment.

choices.text: It cuts waste and saves money over time.
It eliminates the need for packaging entirely.

questions.explanation: The passage says reusable packaging cuts waste and lowers waste management costs, and that supporters see long-term environmental and financial savings. Choice C combines both. A is the reverse of the stated result, since customer loyalty becomes stronger. B is the critics' concern about initial expense, which supporters say is outweighed, so it is a drawback, not a benefit. D exaggerates; containers are reused, not eliminated. Exam tip: for 'benefit' questions, ignore the drawback sentence that follows words like 'while' or 'critics'.
questions.hint: Separate benefits from drawbacks. Words like 'while critics note' introduce the downside, so look for what supporters say instead.

questions.explanation: The relationship is part to whole. A page is one of the parts that make up a book, and a petal is one of the parts that make up a flower. Stem (A) is another part of the flower, not a whole the petal belongs to; a petal is not part of a stem. Garden (C) contains flowers, so a petal belongs to it only indirectly, through the flower. Bee (D) is a visitor to flowers and has no part-to-whole link with petals. Exam tip: in part-to-whole items, choose the immediate whole, the one the part directly belongs to. Reject sibling parts (stem) and larger containers (garden).
questions.hint: Use 'A ___ is a part of a ___.' Reject another part of the same whole (stem) and anything much bigger (garden). Pick the immediate whole.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why are city green spaces becoming more common?
questions.passage: Urban planners are adding green spaces to cities as a response to the growing need for recreation, cleaner air, and heat reduction. These areas provide residents with places to relax, exercise, and escape the built environment. Advocates say green spaces also improve mental health and social cohesion.

choices.text: To offer more industrial development sites
To enhance recreation and environmental benefits.

questions.explanation: The reasons are given in the first sentence: planners respond to the growing need for recreation, cleaner air, and heat reduction. Choice C summarizes these (recreation plus environmental benefits). A, B, and D all contradict the passage, since green spaces are for relaxing and exercising, not traffic, industry, or discouraging outdoor activity. Exam tip: for 'why' questions, look for cause phrases such as 'as a response to', 'because', and 'in order to'.
questions.hint: Find the cause phrase 'as a response to' in the first sentence and match its list of needs to the choices. Reject any choice that contradicts the passage.

questions.explanation: The relationship is structure or vehicle to the space it crosses. A bridge crosses over water; an airplane crosses through the sky. Runway (B) is the surface used for takeoff and landing, not the space the airplane travels through. Airport (C) is a facility. River (D) is a trap: it is a kind of water, so it belongs with the first pair and not with the airplane. Exam tip: the answer must belong to the airplane's side of the analogy, so avoid choices that echo the first pair.
questions.hint: Complete the sentence: 'A bridge crosses ___; an airplane crosses ___.' Reject choices that belong to the bridge side (like river) or to takeoff and landing.

questions.prompt: What is the main environmental concern described in the passage?
questions.passage: Coastal communities face rising sea levels and stronger storms. Many residents are investing in storm barriers and elevated homes, but the costs remain a serious challenge. Experts warn that without changes to emissions and planning, floods may become more frequent and damaging.

choices.text: Rising sea levels and storm damage

questions.explanation: The first sentence states the threat directly: rising sea levels and stronger storms. The rest of the passage supports it: barriers and elevated homes are responses, and experts warn of more frequent and damaging floods. A (air pollution) and D (deforestation) are never mentioned. B (coastal erosion) is the tempting one because it fits the setting, but the passage does not discuss it. Exam tip: answer only from the passage and do not bring in outside knowledge, even if it is true.
questions.hint: Find the problem named in the first sentence and confirm it is repeated in later sentences. Reject choices that merely sound related to coasts or the environment.

questions.explanation: The relationship is male to female counterpart of the same rank. A queen is the female counterpart of a king, and an empress is the female counterpart of an emperor. Prince (A) and duke (D) are male titles of lower rank. King (C) is male and of a different rank, so it matches the first word, not the second. Exam tip: in gender-pair analogies, check both gender and rank or role.
questions.hint: Ask 'What is the female counterpart of an emperor?' Eliminate male titles and titles of a different rank.

questions.prompt: What is the author's attitude toward the new technology?
questions.passage: The article notes that the new device increases accessibility while also raising concerns about privacy. Users appreciate the convenience, but some are wary of how much personal data the system collects. The writer suggests that regulation may be needed to balance innovation with user rights.
questions.explanation: The author acknowledges real benefits (accessibility, convenience) and real worries (privacy, data collection), then suggests regulation to balance the two. That mix of approval and care is 'cautiously optimistic'. A and B are one-sided extremes, and the passage contains both positive and negative points. D is wrong because the writer clearly cares enough to propose a solution. Exam tip: when a passage has both praise and concern, the answer is usually a balanced attitude (cautious, measured, mixed). One-sided passages produce one-sided answers.
questions.hint: List the positive points and the negative points. If both are present, reject 'completely' or 'entirely' choices and pick the balanced tone.

questions.explanation: The relationship is antonyms. Silent means making no sound, and loud is its opposite. Scarce means insufficient or hard to find, so its opposite is abundant, meaning present in large quantity. Rare (A) and limited (B) are synonyms of scarce, so they repeat the idea instead of reversing it. Valuable (C) is the association trap: scarce things often cost more, but valuable describes worth, not quantity, and it is not the opposite of scarce. Exam tip: when the first pair is opposites, cross out the synonyms first, then reject words that are merely associated with the given word.
questions.hint: Confirm the first pair is opposites. Cross out the two synonyms of SCARCE, then ask whether the remaining word reverses its meaning (quantity) or only goes along with it (value).

questions.prompt: What is one drawback the passage mentions about remote work?
questions.passage: Remote work can boost flexibility and reduce commuting, but it may also blur the boundary between home and work. Employees can struggle to disconnect, and employers may find it harder to maintain team cohesion. Effective policies are needed to support remote arrangements without causing burnout.
questions.explanation: The pivot word 'but' introduces the downsides: the boundary between home and work blurs, and employees struggle to disconnect. That matches C. A and B reverse the stated benefits, since remote work boosts flexibility and reduces commuting. D (lower employee autonomy) is never mentioned. The passage also mentions harder team cohesion for employers, but that is not offered as a choice. Exam tip: contrast words (but, however, while, although, yet) separate benefits from drawbacks, so use them to find the right half of the sentence.
questions.hint: Locate the contrast word 'but'. Benefits come before it and drawbacks after it. Reject choices that reverse a stated benefit.

questions.explanation: The relationship is tool to its primary function. A spoon is used mainly to eat, and a pen is used mainly to write. Draw (B) is a secondary use, since a pen can draw but that is not what it is chiefly for. Paint (D) is done with brushes, and cut (C) with blades or scissors. Exam tip: when two choices seem to fit a tool, choose its primary, defining function, the one the tool is named or designed for.
questions.hint: Ask 'What is a pen mainly for?' When more than one action fits, pick the primary function, not a possible side use.

questions.explanation: The relationship is workplace to the professional who works there. A doctor practices in a hospital; a judge presides in a court. Teacher (B) works in a school. Patient (C) and client (D) are people who come to a place to receive a service, not professionals who work there. Patient is the direct counterpart trap, since it is associated with hospital. Exam tip: check whether the second word is the one who provides the service or the one who receives it.
questions.hint: Ask 'Who works here and carries out its main function?' Remove people who only visit or receive services.

questions.prompt: What is the main concern mentioned about single-use plastics?
questions.passage: Single-use plastics are convenient but create lasting environmental problems because they take hundreds of years to decompose. Many cities are banning these items to reduce pollution in oceans and landfills. Critics say alternatives must be affordable and scalable to make the ban effective.

choices.text: They are too cheap to produce.
They are not useful for packaging.

questions.explanation: The concern about the plastics themselves is in the first sentence: they take hundreds of years to decompose, creating lasting environmental problems and pollution in oceans and landfills. That is B. A is never stated. C contradicts the passage, which calls them convenient. D is never mentioned. Note that the critics' point about affordable alternatives is about whether the ban will work, not a concern about plastics. Exam tip: separate what a passage says about the topic itself from what it says about proposed solutions.
questions.hint: The question asks about the plastics, not the bans. Find the 'but' that introduces their problem and ignore the critics' comment about bans.

questions.explanation: The relationship is individual unit to the group it forms. Many trees make a forest, and many stars make a galaxy. Planet (B) is a different kind of body, not a group of stars. Universe (C) does contain stars, but it is the largest whole and holds galaxies themselves, so it is too broad. Solar system (D) is built around a single star plus its planets, not a large group of stars. Exam tip: match the scale. The answer should be the immediate group, not the largest whole.
questions.hint: Ask 'What is a large group of stars called?' Pick the immediate group, not the biggest possible container.

questions.prompt: Which phrase best describes the author's tone in the passage?
questions.passage: The article celebrates community gardens as places where neighbors grow food together, share stories, and support one another. The author notes that these gardens create a sense of belonging and also provide fresh produce in urban neighborhoods.
questions.explanation: Words like 'celebrates', 'support', 'belonging', and 'fresh produce' carry a warm, approving feel, so the tone is appreciative and positive. A and B describe negative attitudes that have no support in the passage; B is also self-contradictory, since hostile and indifferent are opposite attitudes. D describes the style of the writing, not the author's attitude toward the subject, and the passage is not especially formal or academic anyway. Exam tip: tone questions are answered by underlining emotionally charged words, and a tone answer should describe feeling, not writing style.
questions.hint: Underline the feeling words (celebrates, support, belonging). Are they positive or negative? Reject choices that describe writing style instead of attitude.

questions.explanation: The relationship is the person who guides to the person being guided. A parent guides and raises a child, and a teacher guides and instructs a student. Principal (B) is a supervisor of the teacher, which reverses the direction of authority. Lesson (C) is what is taught, not a person. School (D) is the place where teaching happens. Exam tip: check direction. The second word should be the one who receives guidance, not someone above the first word or a thing.
questions.hint: Ask 'Who is taught or guided by a teacher?' Reject people above the teacher, things, and places.

questions.prompt: What problem does the passage say can be reduced by better public transit?
questions.passage: Improving public transit helps reduce traffic congestion, air pollution, and commuting costs. When more people choose buses and trains over cars, cities see fewer vehicles on the road and cleaner air in the downtown core.
questions.explanation: The first sentence lists three problems reduced by better transit: traffic congestion, air pollution, and commuting costs. Only traffic congestion appears among the choices, so C is correct, and the second sentence supports it with 'fewer vehicles on the road'. Noise pollution (D) is the near-miss trap, since the passage mentions air pollution, not noise pollution. A and B are never mentioned. Exam tip: when a passage lists several items, the correct choice is often just one of them, and a similar-sounding choice may not be in the list at all.
questions.hint: List the problems named in the first sentence, then find the choice that matches one of them word for word. Watch for look-alike terms, such as noise pollution versus air pollution.

questions.explanation: The relationship is instrument to the kind of object it is used to observe. A microscope is used to view tiny things, and a telescope is used to view far (distant) things. Close (A) is the opposite of what a telescope is for. Bright (C) is a quality of some objects but not what defines a telescope's use. Small (D) is a trap: it is a synonym of tiny, so it repeats the microscope's side of the analogy. Exam tip: the answer should describe what the third word's instrument is for, not echo the second word.
questions.hint: Ask 'What kind of thing do you point a telescope at?' Cross out synonyms of TINY, because they belong to the microscope.

questions.prompt: Which benefit of exercise is emphasized in the passage?
questions.passage: Regular exercise improves mood by releasing endorphins and reducing stress. People who exercise often report feeling more energetic and less anxious after physical activity.
questions.explanation: Both sentences focus on mental and emotional benefits: improved mood, reduced stress, more energy, and less anxiety. That is B. A (lower cholesterol), C (muscle mass), and D (sprint speed) are physical benefits that never appear in the passage; C is also weakened by the word 'only'. Exam tip: 'emphasized' means the idea repeated or stressed in the passage, so choose what is stated, not what is true in general.
questions.hint: Which idea appears in both sentences? Reject benefits that are true in real life but are not mentioned in the passage.

questions.explanation: The relationship is a work to the action used to take it in. A book is read, and music is listened to. Write (B) and compose (C) are actions of creating, not of experiencing, so they reverse the direction (compare item 1, creator to creation). Speak (D) is about producing words, not receiving music. Exam tip: check direction. Are you asking how the work is made or how it is received? Read is a receiving action, so the answer must also be a receiving action.
questions.hint: Ask 'What do you do with music once it exists?' Reject creating actions (write, compose) because READ is about receiving, not making.

questions.explanation: The relationship is quantity to its standard unit of measurement. A kilogram is a standard unit used to measure weight, and a liter is a standard unit used to measure volume. Carat (B) is also a unit, but it measures the weight (mass) of gemstones, not volume. Intensity (C) is a property that can be measured, not a unit. Quantity (D) is a general term for an amount, not a specific unit.
questions.hint: Ask: 'What unit is used to measure the second word's counterpart?' Look for a unit, not another property. Eliminate any choice that is a unit of something other than volume.

questions.explanation: The relationship is action to the professional who performs it. Titration is a laboratory procedure carried out by a chemist, and installation of wiring, fixtures, and systems is carried out by an electrician. Equipment (B) is what gets installed, which is the object of the action. Office (C) is a place, not a performer. Appointee (D) is the person who is installed into a position, so it is the recipient of the action, not the doer. Always check whether the first word's partner is a doer or a receiver, then match it.
questions.hint: Titrate → who does it? A chemist, the person performing the action. Find the person who performs 'install', not the thing installed.

questions.explanation: The relationship is emotion or purpose to the literary form that expresses it. An ode is a lyric poem written to praise or celebrate its subject, and an elegy is a poem written to lament the dead or express sorrow. An epic (A) is a long narrative poem about heroic deeds. A tale (C) is a simple story with no specific emotional purpose. A romance (D) is a narrative of love or adventure. Memory aid: ode = praise, elegy = lament or mourning, epic = heroes, ballad = story in song.
questions.hint: Which poem form is written to express grief or mourning, just as an ode is written to express praise? Know your literary forms: ode, elegy, epic, sonnet, ballad.

questions.explanation: The relationship is tool to its function. A blowtorch is used to weld (join metal with heat), and a drill is used to bore (make a hole). Fasten (A), screw (B), and rivet (C) all belong to the family of joining or attaching. They are things done with a screwdriver, rivet gun, or similar tools, not with a drill. Note that a weld is itself a way of joining, so the three joining-related distractors are traps for those who match 'weld' too loosely. Match the tool's own action, not the category of the second word.
questions.hint: Ask: what is a drill primarily used to do? It makes holes. Which choice means to make a hole?

questions.explanation: The relationship is a revered figure to the admiration or response directed toward them. A hero is met with adulation (intense, often excessive admiration), and a saint is met with reverence (deep respect and veneration). Asceticism (A), humility (C), and celibacy (D) are qualities or practices a saint may have, but they are not what is given to a saint. The test is direction: adulation is given to the hero, so look for the feeling given to the saint, not a trait the saint possesses.
questions.hint: Is 'adulation' something a hero has or something a hero receives? Find the word that fits the same direction for a saint.

questions.explanation: The relationship is unit to the whole it forms. Vertebrae are the individual bones that, joined together, make up the spine, and links are the individual rings that, joined together, make up a chain. The other choices are traps built on other meanings of 'links'. Cuff (A) comes from 'cufflinks', which are fasteners, not parts that form a cuff. Golf (B) uses the meaning 'links' = a golf course, a different sense of the word. Union (C) is an abstract result of linking, not a physical whole made of links. Exam tip: many words have several meanings. Pick the meaning that fits the first pair (parts of a body structure leads to parts of a physical structure) and reject answers that use a different sense of the word.
questions.hint: Say it as 'Vertebrae are the individual parts of a spine, so links are the individual parts of a ___.' Watch for answers that use a different meaning of 'links'.

questions.explanation: The relationship is action to what it takes away or diminishes. To darken is to deprive something of light, and to suppress (in the sense of oppress or hold down) is to deprive people of freedom. Both verbs remove something desirable. Crime (A) and slavery (B) are things people want suppressed, so the verb would be doing something good, which breaks the parallel with darken. Justice (D) is desirable, but 'freedom' is the classic object of suppress (suppress speech, suppress dissent, suppress liberty) and fits better. Exam tip: when several choices are grammatically possible, check the tone of the first pair. Darken takes away something positive, so the answer should name something positive that is taken away.
questions.hint: Ask 'What does darkening remove, and is it something good or bad?' Light is something good, so find a good thing that suppressing removes. Reject bad things that people want suppressed (crime, slavery).

questions.explanation: The relationship is an event to its scheduled break. An intermission is a planned pause during a concert, and a recess is a planned pause during a trial. Summation (A, the closing arguments), defense (B), and interrogation (C, questioning of a witness) are all active stages of a trial, not breaks from it. They are the trap for anyone who matches 'parts of a trial' instead of 'a pause in the event'. Exam tip: first name the relationship precisely. 'A pause or break in' is more specific than 'something that happens during', and it eliminates every active stage.
questions.hint: An intermission is a pause, not a performance. Find the pause in a trial and reject choices that are stages of the trial itself.

questions.explanation: The relationship is a gesture to the feeling it expresses. Applause is a way of showing praise, and a curtsy is a courteous gesture of respect or deference, traditionally to a monarch, a superior, or a guest of honor. Exit (A) is an action but not a feeling a curtsy expresses. Servility (B) means excessive, groveling submission, which is far stronger and more negative than a curtsy. Obedience (C) is following orders, which a gesture of courtesy does not show. Exam tip: match both the type and the intensity of the feeling. Praise is a moderate, positive feeling, so the answer should also be moderate and positive.
questions.hint: Ask 'What feeling does this gesture show?' A curtsy is polite and courteous, not groveling or commanding. Reject choices that are too strong or about orders.

questions.explanation: The relationship is a person to the quality that defines them. A patriot is, by definition, loyal to their country, and a scholar is, by definition, erudite, meaning deeply learned through extensive study. Skeptic (A) is a noun naming a type of person, not a quality, so it is the wrong part of speech; the answer must be an adjective like loyal. Intelligent (C) is too general: a person can be intelligent without being a scholar, and a scholar's defining mark is depth of learning, not raw intelligence. Studious (B) is the closest competitor. It describes a habit of diligent study, which a schoolchild can have without being a scholar, so it does not define a scholar the way erudite does. Exam tip: when two adjectives seem to fit, ask which one the person must have to deserve the label. A patriot who is not loyal is not a patriot, and a scholar who is not learned is not a scholar. Vocabulary note: erudite = having or showing great knowledge gained from books and study.
questions.hint: The second word is an adjective, so reject the noun (skeptic) first. Then ask which adjective a person must have to be called a scholar, just as a patriot must be loyal. Prefer the quality that defines the role over a habit or a general trait.

questions.explanation: The relationship is tool to the action it performs directly on its target. A hammer pounds, and a spear pierces. Kill (C) is a possible result, just as pounding may result in a driven nail. The analogy needs the tool's action, not its outcome. Hunt (D) is an activity in which a spear is used, so it is the purpose, not the action. Exam tip: separate the tool's own action (pound, pierce) from how it is delivered (throw), what it achieves (kill), and why it is used (hunt).

questions.explanation: The relationship is category to a specific example of it. A sundial is one kind of timepiece, and television is one kind of medium (media is the plural). questions.explanation: The relationship is remedy to the problem it relieves. Water relieves thirst, and a salve soothes a wound. Levy (A) is a tax or charge imposed on people, and fine (B) is a penalty for breaking a rule; neither is a guarantee. Reparation (D) is compensation paid after damage has already happened, so it goes with the damage side of the first pair and not with a bond. Exam tip: this is a loose item, so use elimination. questions.explanation: The relationship is an activity to the plan that lays out what will happen during it. Destination (B) is where a trip ends, not a plan of it. Schedule (C) is the closest competitor, but it is a general term for any set of times, while 'itinerary' is the plan made specifically for a journey, just as 'agenda' is the plan made specifically for a meeting. questions.explanation: The relationship is a ruler to the people or territory they govern. Church (A) is led by clergy, embassy (C) by an ambassador, and consulate (D) by a consul. Those are officials of other kinds, not rulers of a territory. questions.explanation: The relationship is a product to the process that defines how it is made. Brewing (A) is the process for making beer. Frothing (B) is forming foam and is not a production process. questions.passage:
"Thou canst not stir a flower without troubling of a star," stated the mystical poet Francis Thompson. He exaggerated the links in the fabric of life, but his was, nonetheless, a true insight into the fact that there do exist ecological relationships between living things here on earth and the movements of the heavenly bodies. Not only are earthly organisms affected by light and warmth from the distant moon and sun, but many animals have also been shown to possess mechanisms which accurately measure the sun's position and react to the rhythm of the tides, the phases of the moon, and the motion of our planet.


Twice each day, at dusk and at dawn, there is a shift in the activity of the population that inhabits a community, amounting to almost a complete turnover of the species. Some kinds of plants and animals are stimulated to activity by light; other kinds retreat from it. The varying amounts of light and darkness act as triggers upon the physiology of numerous kinds of animals and plants, signaling them to many activities.


Many forms of life display fairly definite tendencies towards daytime or nighttime activity and many animals can alter their pattern in response to changing needs. In regions where game is hunted persistently, the hunted animals tend to become nocturnal, whereas the same species is diurnal in areas where man has not made deep inroads. Man, as an animal, also apparently possesses a number of built-in rhythms, and his body chemistry has been shown to operate in a rhythmic pattern.

there exists a relationship between living things and the universe
some life-forms are largely unaffected by the heavenly bodies

questions.explanation: The line is figurative. A flower stands for living things on earth, and a star stands for the heavenly bodies, so the line says that what happens to one affects the other. The rest of the paragraph backs this up with examples, such as organisms affected by light and warmth from the moon and sun and animals that react to tides and moon phases. Choice A takes the line as advice about how to behave, but the passage never tells anyone to avoid disturbing nature. Choice C reads 'flower' literally and narrows the meaning to one kind of living thing, and the passage says nothing about handling plants carefully. Choice D is the opposite of the passage, which says earthly organisms are affected by the sun and moon. Exam tip: when a passage quotes a figurative statement, the writer's next sentence usually explains it, so find that explanation and match your answer to it. Do not take the symbols literally.

questions.prompt: The main purpose of the author in writing the selection is to show
questions.passage:
Gitanjali (1961-1977), terminally ill of cancer at 16, wrote one hundred eleven (111) poems in English, most of them about death. Not wishing to alarm her mother, she kept her poems. It was only several months after her death that her mother, Khushi Badruddin, discovered that her daughter was India's Emily Dickinson.


The comparison with the American poet is inevitable, since both women wrote secretly about death, nature, and God. Gitanjali likens death to an "honoured guest," as Dickinson does in "Because I Could Not Stop for Death." Gitanjali's grammatical lapses, in fact, recall those of Dickinson's. But the similarities stop there, because Gitanjali was actually facing death.


Although love of life sometimes overpowers her, Gitanjali repeatedly welcomes death "with open arms." This is not mere resignation. The poet feels that with more time on earth, she may end up having less faith in God. Dying young seems to assure salvation. The poems are indeed deeply religious; many of them are prayers. Gitanjali's parents are Sikhs, and she attended a Catholic school, but she always said her religion was love.


Curiously, some of the poems speak of the poet in the third person, as though Gitanjali was looking at herself objectively. She writes "Illness too is / A gift of God / And Gitanjali accepts it / With grace and in good stride." Perhaps, the strain had become too strong even for the brave young poet. Gitanjali means "song-offering," and the whole volume is an offering of songs to God about what it means to die so young.

choices.text: the similarities between Dickinson's and Gitanjali's poems
Gitanjali's sentiments towards death as expressed in her poems

questions.prompt: What conclusion can be deduced from the second paragraph?
questions.passage:
Television, radio, and stereo can be vehicles for great drama, beautiful music, or even redeeming words. But who can claim that for the vast majority of people, these devices are anything other than agents of noise? They are not listened to; they are only heard.


Modern man begins his day with radio noise to wake him up, he has a car radio or CD player to carry him to his work, continues with pipe-in music in the elevator and "on hold" on the office telephone, relaxes by the videoke at the bar, and concludes his day with television chatter. Those who cannot sleep in the silence that descends when the TV is shut off resort to machines that produce "white noise."


Silence has become a vacuum which modern man abhors. It is no longer normal or good in itself. It is understood only as absence of noise. Before noise (B.N.), there were sounds distinguishable from noise, because sounds came out of silence. Silence was the background for sounds.


City dwellers, awash in constant noise, become nervous in the country because the sounds of the country – from the crickets, birds, and animals – are made against the background of silence. There is also less talk in the country because to interrupt the silence, one must have something to say.


In the city, words are part of the general noise – one can say anything in order not to stop talking – and silence is always interpreted as awkwardness. There seems to be a fear that if the noise stops, the city will collapse in silence.


Before the days of widespread TV, the Swiss thinker, Max Picard, offered the notion that people play the radio to make sure that they are still there. This proposition neatly reverses the old conundrum: If a tree falls in a forest, does it make a sound if there is no one there to hear it? This question presumes man exists and asks if sound exists without man's hearing it. The modern form of this question, à la Picard, would reverse these presumptions and have modern man asking, "If there is no noise, how do I know I am really here?"


Solitude and silence are the crucibles of serious thought. To flee them is to flee the conditions necessary for the self-examination that makes life worth living. It is to flee as well the peace that comes only from the orientation of one's life to the ultimate realities – realities that can intrude only when one is still and quiet and open to them.


I am often told that people turn on the radio and television because they are lonely. Noise is used as a tonic for loneliness. It is an acoustic drug. But loneliness is a longing for something which should not be drowned in noise. If one quietly searches for loneliness, one can begin to ask why one is lonely and for what. Loneliness lets us know that we really have nothing adequate for our deepest longing – not in our friends, not in our family, nor in our worldly goods or pleasures.


In what then or in whom are we to find the object of our deepest desire? This is perhaps the most important question that can be asked, and it can be answered only in SILENCE.

Man depends on sounds to keep him functioning.
Man likes inventions because these are signs of progress.
Man finds complete relaxation only when surrounded by noise.

questions.explanation: A conclusion is an idea that follows from the details, not one the paragraph states outright. The second paragraph walks through a whole day: radio noise to wake up, a car radio or CD player on the way to work, piped-in music in the elevator and on the phone, the videoke bar to relax, television at night, and 'white noise' machines for people who cannot sleep in silence. Sound surrounds every part of the day, from waking to working to relaxing to sleeping, so the conclusion is that man depends on it to function. Choice A only repeats the surface of the list; the paragraph is about dependence, not about loving machines, and the first paragraph calls these devices 'agents of noise.' Choice C is never mentioned, since the paragraph does not discuss progress or invention. Choice D goes too far: the paragraph says he relaxes at the videoke bar, but 'complete relaxation' and 'only' are claims the paragraph does not make, and the author goes on to argue that peace comes from silence. Buddhism is both a philosophy and a practice. Buddhist philosophy is rich and profound. Buddhist practice is called Tantra, a Sanskrit word meaning "to weave."


Buddhist philosophy reached its ultimate development in the second century A.D. No one has been able to improve much on it since then. The distinction between Buddhist philosophy and Tantra is well defined. Buddhist philosophy can be intellectualized, Tantra cannot. Buddhist philosophy is a function of the rational mind, Tantra transcends rationality.


The most profound thinkers of the Indian civilization discovered that words and concepts can take them only so far. Beyond that point came the actual doing of a practice, the experience of which was ineffable. This did not prevent them from progressively refining the practice into an extremely effective and sophisticated set of techniques, but it did prevent them from being able to describe the experience which the techniques produce.


The practice of Tantra does not mean the end of rational thought. It means the integration of thought based on symbols into larger spectrums of awareness.


The development of Buddhism in India shows that a profound and penetrating intellectual quest into the ultimate nature of reality can culminate in, or at least, set the stage for, a quantum leap beyond rationality. In fact, on an individual level, this is one of the roads to enlightenment. Tibetan Buddhism calls it the Path without Form or the Practice of the Mind. The Path without Form is prescribed for the people of intellectual temperament. The science of physics is following a similar path.


The development of physics in the twentieth century has already transformed the consciousness of those involved with it. The study of complementarity, the uncertainty principle, the quantum field theory, and the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics produce insights into the nature of reality very similar to those produced by the study of Eastern philosophy. The profound physicists of this century have increasingly become aware that they are confronting the ineffable.


Max Planck, the father of quantum mechanics, wrote "Science . . . means unresting endeavor and continually progressing development toward an aim which the poetic intuition may apprehend, but which the intellect can never fully grasp." We are approaching "the end of science." "The end of science" does not mean the end of "unresting endeavor and continually progressing development" of more and more comprehensive and useful physical theories. "The end of science" means the coming of Western civilization, in its own time and in its own way, into the higher dimensions of human experience.

questions.explanation: The relationship is a body structure to the organ system it belongs to. The alveoli are the tiny air sacs of the lungs where oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged, so they belong to the respiratory system. The ventricles are the two lower chambers of the heart that pump blood out to the lungs and the body, so they belong to the circulatory system. Endocrine (A) is the system of hormone-producing glands, and digestive (C) is the system of the stomach and intestines; neither has ventricles. Nervous (D) is the trap: the brain also has fluid-filled cavities called ventricles, but when the word is used on its own, it usually means the chambers of the heart. Exam tip: for structure-to-system items, name the organ first (alveoli: lungs; ventricles: heart) and then name its system.
questions.hint: Ask 'Which organ is this structure part of, and which system does that organ belong to?' Alveoli are in the lungs; ventricles are chambers of the heart. Watch out for the brain's ventricles, which are the lesser-known meaning.

questions.explanation: The relationship is opposites of position: top and bottom. The head is at the top of the body and the feet are at the bottom. A stalactite is the mineral formation that hangs from the ceiling of a cave, and a stalagmite is the formation that rises from the floor, so it is the opposite in position. Icicle (A) is the lookalike trap, because icicles also hang from above, so it goes with the stalactite and not against it. Limestone (B) is the rock in which caves form, and calcium (C) is the mineral from which both formations are built, so both are materials, not opposites. Memory aid: stalaCtites hang from the Ceiling, stalaGmites grow from the Ground.
questions.hint: Is this a top-and-bottom pair? Ask where a stalactite is found (hanging from the ceiling) and what grows from the opposite end (the floor). Reject lookalikes (icicle) and materials (limestone, calcium).

questions.explanation: The relationship is something intended to the step that carries it out. A goal is only reached through action, and a policy is only made real through implementation, which means putting it into effect. Formulation (A) is drafting the policy, which comes before it exists, so it is the start, not the carrying out. Presentation (B) is announcing or explaining the policy, and a policy can be presented without ever being carried out. Evaluation (D) is judging the results afterward. Exam tip: learn the order of the policy process (formulation, presentation or adoption, implementation, evaluation) and ask which stage matches 'action' for a goal, the stage where the plan is acted on.
questions.hint: A goal becomes real through action. What makes a policy real? Reject the stages that come before (formulation, presentation) and after (evaluation) the actual doing.

questions.explanation: The relationship is a professional to the main tool of the trade, the one used to do the core work of cutting. A chef's essential tool is the knife, and a surgeon's is the scalpel, a small, very sharp blade used to make incisions. Anesthesia (A) is a drug or method for numbing or putting the patient to sleep, usually given by an anesthesiologist, and it is not a tool for cutting. Bandage (C) is a supply used to cover a wound afterward, by many people besides surgeons. Gloves (D) are protective gear worn by many professionals, including chefs, and not the instrument that defines the work. Exam tip: match the function as well as the person. The knife cuts food, so the answer is the instrument that cuts tissue.
questions.hint: Ask 'What is the one tool this professional cannot do the core work without?' Choose the one that cuts, like the knife, and reject supplies, drugs, and protective gear.

questions.explanation: The relationship is a tool to its primary function. A scalpel is used to cut, and forceps are pincer-like instruments used to grasp and hold things, such as tissue, a needle, or a dressing. Transfuse (A) means to give blood, which is done through an intravenous line, not with forceps. Remove (B) is a possible outcome, because forceps can be used to lift out a splinter or a foreign object, but the tool's own action is to hold, and removing is what is done with that hold. Retract (C) means to pull tissue back to keep a surgical opening clear, and that job belongs to retractors, a different surgical instrument and the trap for those thinking of surgical tools. Exam tip: compare item 21 (pen : write). Choose the tool's defining action, not what it is sometimes used to accomplish.
questions.hint: Ask what forceps do with their two arms: they grip. Choose that action, and reject the result (remove), the job of another instrument (retract), and an action done through a different device (transfuse).

questions.explanation: The relationship is a remedy to the condition it is used to treat (compare item 44, water : thirst :: salve : wound). A sedative is given to soothe pain and distress, and an antiseptic is applied to a wound to kill germs and prevent infection. Emergency (A) is a situation, not a condition that an antiseptic treats. Anxiety (B) is a trap for the second pair: it is what a sedative actually calms, so it belongs on the sedative side, and an antiseptic does nothing for it. Fracture (C) is a broken bone, which is treated with a splint or a cast, and an antiseptic does not mend bone. Vocabulary note: strictly, a sedative calms nervousness or induces sleep, and the drug that relieves pain is an analgesic. The item uses 'sedative' loosely. Exam tip: when the first pair is a little imprecise, state the relationship in a general form (remedy to what it treats) and apply it to the second pair.
questions.hint: Use 'A ___ is used on / for ___.' An antiseptic is applied to something that has been broken open. Reject choices that are situations, or conditions that need a different treatment.

questions.explanation: The relationship is a substance to the word that describes how it flows. Vinegar is thin and flows easily, so it is runny. Ketchup is thick and flows slowly, so it is viscous, which means resistant to flow (viscosity is the resistance of a fluid to flowing). Turbid (A) means cloudy or muddy, a description of clarity and not of thickness, and a thin liquid can be turbid (muddy water). Motile (B) means able to move on its own, as bacteria and sperm cells do. Pectinous (D) means containing or resembling pectin, the gel-forming substance in fruit used to set jam, and it is the lookalike vocabulary trap. Exam tip: hard vocabulary choices are often there to scare you. Define the word you know (viscous: thick and slow-flowing) and use the others only to eliminate. Related: honey and syrup are viscous.
questions.hint: Ask what property vinegar has (thin, flows easily) and what the opposite property of ketchup is (thick, slow). Know the words: viscous = thick and slow-flowing, turbid = cloudy, motile = able to move.

questions.explanation: The relationship is synonyms, with the second word stronger than the first. Passionate is a more intense form of enthusiastic. In the same way, abundant, meaning present in very large quantity, is a step up from plentiful. Scant (B) and minimal (C) are antonyms, since they mean very little, so they reverse the idea. Ample (D) is the closest competitor, because it is also a synonym of plentiful, but it means enough or more than enough and is not stronger than plentiful, so it does not repeat the step up in intensity. Exam tip: when two choices are synonyms, check whether the first pair also changes in degree (enthusiastic to passionate is a step up) and choose the one that matches.
questions.hint: First confirm the pair is synonyms, and cross out the two antonyms (scant, minimal). Then ask whether the second word is stronger than the first, and choose the synonym that is also a step up.

questions.explanation: The relationship is a protective outer layer to the organ it protects. The sclera is the tough white outer coat of the eyeball that protects its delicate inner structures and gives it shape, and the cranium is the bony case of the skull that encloses and protects the brain. Scalp (A) is the skin that covers the cranium, so it is on the same side as the cranium and not what the cranium protects. Bone (B) names what kind of thing the cranium is, which is a different relationship (type of). Head (C) is the closest competitor, since the cranium is a part of the head, but 'head' also includes the face, jaw, and skin, and the cranium specifically exists to protect what is inside it. Exam tip: when two relationships both seem to work (part to whole, or protector to protected), choose the one that fits the defining job of the structure, and for a skull part that is to protect the brain.
questions.hint: Ask 'What does a cranium protect?' Reject what covers the cranium from the outside (scalp), what category it belongs to (bone), and the broad part-to-whole choice (head).

questions.explanation: The relationship is a quality to the thing it describes. We call reasoning (logic) valid or invalid, depending on whether its structure holds together, and we call a fact or statement true or false, depending on whether it matches reality. So the word that goes with true is fact. False (A) is the opposite of true, so it is the antonym trap and does not name a thing that can be true. Argument (C) is the trap that comes from the first pair: an argument is judged valid or invalid, not true or false, so it goes with 'valid.' Reason (D) is a near-synonym of logic, so it belongs on the first side of the analogy. Exam tip: ask 'What do we call true?' (a fact or statement) and 'What do we call valid?' (an argument or piece of reasoning). The two words are not interchangeable in logic.
questions.hint: Ask what we describe as valid (reasoning, logic) and what we describe as true (a fact or statement). Reject the opposite of true (false) and the words that go with 'valid' (argument, reason).

questions.explanation: The relationship is a remedy to the suffering it eases. To comfort is to ease an affliction (a source of pain or distress), and a salve is an ointment applied to ease the pain of a wound. Problem (A) is too general: a salve does not solve problems, it soothes a specific physical injury. Fear (B) is the trap on the first side, since comfort can ease fear, but a salve does nothing for it. Tragedy (C) is an event that people may be comforted about, and a salve does not treat an event. Exam tip: when the first pair is abstract (comfort, affliction) and the second is physical (salve), keep the same relationship (a remedy to the thing it eases) and pick the concrete choice the remedy is applied to.
questions.hint: Use 'A ___ eases a(n) ___.' A salve is applied to something physical. Reject abstract words (problem, fear) and events (tragedy).

questions.explanation: The relationship is two different kinds within the same larger group. A drupe is a fruit with a single hard stone inside (peach, cherry, mango), and a pome is a fruit with a fleshy outside and a core of seeds (apple, pear). They are sibling types of fruit, neither of which contains the other. A vegetable is likewise one category of edible plants, and a sibling category beside it is herb (a plant used for flavor or medicine). Mulch (A) is a covering spread over soil, which is not food. Crop (B) is a larger group that includes vegetables, so it reverses the pattern: a vegetable is a kind of crop, but a drupe is not a kind of pome. Bulb (C) names a plant part, and some vegetables (onion, garlic) are bulbs, so a bulb is a kind of vegetable, not a sibling of one. Exam tip: when the first pair are siblings, reject choices that are bigger groups or smaller members of the third word. Vocabulary: drupe = stone fruit; pome = core fruit.
questions.hint: Ask whether the first two words are siblings (two kinds of fruit) or one inside the other. They are siblings, so look for a sibling category of vegetable, and reject any choice that is a bigger group (crop) or a member (bulb).

questions.explanation: This is a loose item, so work by meaning and elimination. To discover something is to find it out, which is to learn it, so the two words are close in meaning. In the same way, to process something is to treat it through a series of steps in order to prepare it for use (process food, process film, process an application). Prepare (C) is the closest in meaning. Work (A) is the nearest competitor, but 'work' is general and does not carry the idea of getting something ready through steps. Apply (B) means to put something to use, which comes after the processing. Pass (D) means to go by or hand over and is not a meaning of process. Exam tip: when an analogy is loose, state each first word's meaning in your own words first (discover: find out; process: treat in steps to get ready) and choose the word nearest to the second meaning.
questions.hint: Define each first word briefly (discover: find out, process: handle in steps to get ready). Choose the word closest in meaning, and reject words that describe a later stage (apply) or another meaning altogether (pass).

questions.explanation: The relationship is antonyms. Precise means exact and clearly stated, and ambiguous means open to more than one meaning, so the two are opposites in clarity. Concise means expressing much in few words, and its opposite is verbose, which means using more words than needed. Profound (B) means deep or far-reaching, and has no link to word count. Narrow (C) describes a limited width or scope. Thorough (D) means complete and careful, and a text can be both thorough and concise, so it is not an opposite. Exam tip: for antonym items, find what scale the word is on (brevity), and choose the word at the other end of that same scale.
questions.hint: Confirm the first pair is opposites. Then ask what CONCISE is about (the number of words used) and choose the word that is the opposite on that same scale.

questions.explanation: The relationship is a feeling or action to a much stronger form of it. To revere is to feel deep, almost worshipful respect, a step beyond ordinary respect. To humiliate is to make someone feel deeply ashamed and lowered in dignity, often in front of others, which is a step beyond shame. Ostracize (A) means to exclude someone from a group, which can follow shame but is a different action. Repudiate (B) means to reject or disown something, such as a claim or a person. Execute (C) means to put to death, or to carry out a plan, and has nothing to do with degrees of shame. Exam tip: a degree-of-intensity analogy keeps the same kind of idea and raises its strength, so avoid choices that change the kind of idea (exclude, reject, kill).
questions.hint: Ask whether the second word is a stronger form of the first (revere is a deeper respect). Choose the word that is a stronger form of shame, and reject words that name a different action.

(1) English is the language of learning. I've known this since before I could go to school. As a toddler, my first study materials were a set of flash cards that my mother used to teach me the English alphabet.


(2) My mother made our home conducive to learning English: all my storybooks and coloring books were in English, and so were the cartoons I watched and the music I listened to. She required me to speak English at home. She even hired tutors to help me learn to read and write in English.


(3) In school I learned to think in English. We used English to learn about numbers, equations and variables. With it we learned about observation and inference, the moon and the stars, monsoons and photosynthesis. With it we learned about shapes and colors, about meter and rhythm. I learned about God in English, and I prayed to Him in English.


(4) Filipino, on the other hand, was always the "other" subject, almost a special subject like PE or Home Economics, except that it was graded the same way as Science, Math, Religion, and English. My classmates and I used to complain about Filipino all the time. Filipino was a chore, like washing the dishes; it was not the language of learning. It was the language we used to speak to the people who washed our dishes.


(5) We used to think learning Filipino was important because it was practical: Filipino was the language of the world outside the classroom. It was the language of the streets: it was how you spoke to the tindera when you went to the tindahan, what you used to tell your katulong when you had an utos, and how you texted manong when you needed "sundo na."


(6) That being said though, I was proud of my proficiency with the language. Filipino was the language I used to speak with my cousins and uncles and grandparents in the province, so I never had much trouble reciting.


(7) It was really only in university that I began to grasp Filipino in terms of language and not just dialect. Filipino was not merely a peculiar variety of language, derived and continuously borrowing from the English and Spanish alphabets; it has its own system, with its own grammar, semantics, sounds, even symbols.


(8) But more significantly, it has its own way of reading, writing, and thinking. There are ideas and concepts unique to Filipino that can never be translated into another. Try translating bayanihan, tagay, kilig or diskarte.


(9) Only recently have I begun to grasp Filipino as the language of identity: the language of emotion, and even of learning. And with this comes the realization that I do, in fact, smell worse than a malansang isda. My own language is foreign to me: I speak, think, read and write primarily in English. To borrow the terminology of Fr. Bulatao, I am a split-level Filipino.


(10) It is neither the language of the classroom and the laboratory, nor the language of the boardroom, the court room, or the operating room. It is not the language of privilege. I may be disconnected from my being Filipino, but with a tongue of privilege I will always have my connections.


(11) So I have my education to thank for making English my mother language.


An excerpt from "Language, Learning, Identity, Privilege" by James Soriano. The Philippine Daily Inquirer. September 10, 2011.

questions.passage:
(1) In the mid-1980s, the world became suddenly aware that the protective ozone shield in the atmosphere was in danger—was, in fact, greatly depleted in a huge "hole" over the frozen wastes of Antarctica. The mysterious stuff called ozone, which until then was known to the public chiefly as an acrid, lung-burning element of smog in overcrowded cities, was being destroyed in the stratosphere by chemicals made and released in the 20th century by humans.


(2) Ozone is a variant form of oxygen, the most life-sustaining gas of all. Under the intense ultraviolet light from the sun at the upper reaches of the earth's atmosphere, normal two-atom molecules of oxygen are split into single atoms—O rather than O2, in chemists' terms. Some of these single-oxygen atoms rejoin with O2 to form ozone, O3. The amount in the stratosphere is very scant, less than ten parts per million (at sea level, the layer would be about as thick as a pane of window glass), but that layer is enough to stop most of the sun's most dangerous ultraviolet rays from reaching the earth's surface, 10 to 30 miles below.


(3) The possibility of ozone destruction by man-made chemicals had been predicted as early as 1974 by two farsighted researchers, F. Sherwood Rowland and Mario J. Molina, at the University of California at Irvine.


(4) Certain industrial gases dubbed as CFCs—chlorofluorocarbons—are so highly stable and inert that they do not react with other substances in nature. They have long been used as coolants in refrigerators and air conditioners, as propellants in aerosol cans, in making foam-plastic objects, such as coffee cups and fast-food containers, and as solvents for cleansing electronic circuit boards and computer chips. But there could be great danger, warned Rowland and Molina, when these same long-lived gases drift to the upper layers of the atmosphere.


(5) In that same region where ozone is created by solar bombardment, the CFCs could break apart, they postulated, freeing chlorine atoms that could attack and destroy ozone molecules by the billions. If these were to deplete the ozone layer around the whole world, it would put all mankind at risk.


An excerpt from "National Geographic Learning Reader: Climate Change Printed Access Card" by National Geographic Learning. Cengage Learning, 2012.
questions.explanation: The manner of presentation is how the writer handles the material. This selection explains: what ozone is and how it forms (second paragraph), what two researchers predicted (third and fifth paragraphs), and what CFCs are and what they are used for (fourth paragraph). It states facts and describes processes without telling the reader what to do or defending a side, so it is informative, which is choice C. Choice A (practical) would give steps or advice on how to do something, such as how to reduce the use of CFCs, and there is none. Choice B (persuasive) would try to move the reader to act or to adopt a view. The passage does mention danger ('warned,' 'at risk'), but it reports what the researchers predicted and never urges the reader to do anything. Choice D (argumentative) would defend a claim against opposing positions, and the passage gives no opposing view. Exam tip: informative writing explains and reports, persuasive writing urges, argumentative writing defends a claim against objections, and practical writing instructs. Warning words alone do not make a passage persuasive.
questions.hint: Ask what the writer is doing: explaining facts, urging action, defending a claim against objections, or giving instructions? Check whether the passage ever tells the reader what to do or answers an opposing view.

The language of threat runs through every paragraph: the shield 'was in danger,' the 'possibility of ozone destruction' had been predicted, there 'could be great danger,' the CFCs 'could break apart,' and the closing sentence says the loss of the layer 'would put all mankind at risk.'
